Its comment was correct, and it caught something my own tests missed. Bounding the advertisement read stopped the memory growth but left the far side still writing, so I'd **traded an OOM for a deadlock**. I reproduced both before fixing:

- **SSH** — hung the full 30s. `cmd.wait()` was called with stdout still open, so the writer filled the pipe and never exited.
- **Remote helper** — hung the full 60s, in `finish()`'s unbounded `io.Copy(io.Discard, p.out)`, exactly as described. My cap error never got a chance to surface.

Fixed in `b6d9adfd`: the SSH read-error path closes stdout before waiting (via the existing `cleanupSSHCommand`), and the helper path uses `cleanup()` instead of `finish()` on error, with `finish()`'s drain now bounded at 1 MiB. =======
- **A packfile object header can no longer request an unbounded allocation.** `ExtractCommitParents` sized its per-object buffer from the size the pack header *declares*, before reading any content. go-git validates only that the size varint does not overflow, so the value is remote-controlled up to `int64`: a 48-byte pack declaring a 128 TiB object produced `fatal error: out of memory` — a Go runtime fatal, not a panic, so an embedding process could not contain it with `recover()`. A 46-byte pack declaring 64 GiB allocated 64 GiB. The declared size is now rejected above 64 MiB (this path reads tree:0-filtered packs, whose objects are commits and tags measured in kilobytes) and otherwise only sizes the initial buffer, capped at 64 KiB, so the allocation tracks bytes actually received. Reachable from ordinary planning: `FetchCommitParents` runs against the source during ancestry checks.

- **SSH repository paths are now shell-quoted in full.** The remote command string is interpreted by the remote login shell, and `shellQuotePath` exempted the segment before the first slash when the path began with `~`, so the remote shell would expand it. A SCP-style URL puts attacker-influenceable text in exactly that position: `git@host:~a;id/repo.git` produced the remote command `git-upload-pack ~a;id/'repo.git'`, executing `id` on the remote host as the authenticated SSH user. This matters wherever only part of the URL is caller-controlled — a repository path templated into a fixed host, or a path arriving from a webhook or config. Quoting costs nothing: `~` expansion does not depend on the shell here, because `git-upload-pack` resolves the path through `enter_repo()`, which interpolates a leading `~` itself (canonical git quotes the whole path for the same reason). Regression tests assert the generated command against a real `/bin/sh`.

- **Credentials embedded in a remote URL are no longer echoed.** `probe` and `fetch` carried `Source.URL`/`Target.URL` verbatim into their results, which are printed to stdout and serialized into `--json` — so `REDACTED`, the standard CI form, put the token in output that automation collects. The URL-parse failure path leaked it too, since `url.Parse` embeds the raw URL in its error. All of these now redact the whole userinfo component via the new `internal/redact` package. HTTP error messages switch from `url.URL.Redacted()` to the same helper: `Redacted()` masks only the password, leaving a token in the *username* position (`https://<token>@host/...` — how GitHub App and PAT URLs are normally written) in the clear. The redaction helper that `convert-sha256` already had is what this generalizes; its unparseable-URL placeholder changes from `<source url redacted>` to `<url redacted>`.

questions.question: For the redirect leak: when /info/refs redirects to a different host and --*-follow-info-refs-redirect is on, what should happen to an explicit --source-token / --target-token?

options.label: Same-site only, else drop (Recommended)
options.description: Forward the token when the redirect target is the same host or a subdomain of the one you typed (Go's own rule for retaining auth headers); drop it otherwise and fall back to the credential helper. Keeps github.com → codeload.github.com style replicas working. Breaks a replica on a genuinely different domain (e.g. *.githubusercontent.com).

options.label: Explicit host allowlist
options.description: New --source-redirect-allow-host / --target-redirect-allow-host flags. The token goes only to hosts you name; empty allowlist means drop. Safest and most explicit, but every deployment using the flag today needs config added or it starts 401ing.

options.label: Bind token to typed host only
options.description: Closest to vanilla git: the explicit token is only ever sent to the host you typed. Cross-host redirect targets get the credential helper or nothing. Simplest to reason about, but any replica needing the same token breaks unless operators add a helper entry.

options.label: Refuse cross-host redirects
options.description: Fail the run with a clear error rather than silently changing hosts. Fails closed and is trivially auditable, but turns a working-today configuration into a hard error.

questions.question: For ref names from the source that fail validation (containing .., control characters, NUL, or a leading dash) — what should git-sync do?

options.label: Skip the ref, warn, continue (Recommended)
options.description: Matches the existing BestEffort model where per-ref problems become warnings. A mirror doesn't halt because upstream has one malformed ref, and the operator sees it in output. Downside: the mirror silently diverges from source for that ref unless someone reads the warning.

options.label: Fail the whole run
options.description: Any invalid ref name aborts. Strongest integrity guarantee and impossible to miss, but one malformed upstream ref stops all mirroring — and you'd find out in production rather than at review time.

options.label: Fail for convert-sha256, skip+warn for sync
options.description: Split by risk: writing to disk (where a bad name escapes refs/) fails hard, while remote-to-remote mirroring warns and continues. More code paths to reason about, but matches where the actual danger is.

## Auth

For GitHub and similar providers, use basic auth with a token as the password.

Auth is resolved in this order:

- explicit CLI flags
- `GITSYNC_*` environment variables
- local `git credential fill` helper lookup for `http` and `https` remotes
- anonymous access

Relevant variables:

- `GITSYNC_SOURCE_TOKEN`
- `GITSYNC_TARGET_TOKEN`
- `GITSYNC_SOURCE_USERNAME` default: `git`
- `GITSYNC_TARGET_USERNAME` default: `git`

Bearer auth is also available:

- `GITSYNC_SOURCE_BEARER_TOKEN`
- `GITSYNC_TARGET_BEARER_TOKEN`

That means local testing against a dummy GitHub repo can reuse your regular Git credential helper setup without passing tokens on every command.

## Protocol Notes

### Credentials and redirects

Credentials you supply explicitly — `--source-token`, `--target-token`, their
bearer equivalents, or userinfo in the URL — are bound to the host you named.
They are sent to that host, and to subdomains of it on the same scheme and port,
and nowhere else.

This matters with `--source-follow-info-refs-redirect` /
`--target-follow-info-refs-redirect`, which send follow-up RPCs to the host that
`/info/refs` redirected to. A redirect within the same site (say `example.com`
to `replica.example.com`, the hosting-replica case the flag exists for) keeps
your credentials. A redirect to an unrelated host does not: git-sync withholds
them, prints a warning naming the host, and consults the git credential helper
for that host instead. So a redirect you did not intend — an open redirect on the
real host, a hostile mirror, or a man-in-the-middle on a plain-`http` source —
cannot collect your token.

If a redirect target legitimately needs credentials and is not same-site, store
them in your git credential helper against that host; git-sync will find them
there.

git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Bind explicit credentials to the host they were configured for

With --source-follow-info-refs-redirect / --target-follow-info-refs-redirect,
git-sync adopts the host /info/refs redirected to and addresses it
directly for the follow-up RPCs — and re-attached the configured token to
those requests, after Go's http.Client had deliberately stripped the
Authorization header on the cross-host hop. Any redirect an attacker
could cause collected the token: an open redirect on the real host, a
hostile mirror, or a man-in-the-middle on a plain-http source. On the
target side that token usually carries write access.

An explicitly supplied credential — token flags, bearer flags, or
userinfo in the URL — is now sent only to the host named on the command
line and its subdomains, on the same scheme and port. Anything else gets
nothing, plus a warning naming the withheld host, and the credential
helper is consulted for that host instead. Credentials resolved *from*
the helper are untouched: those are looked up keyed on the host actually
being challenged, so they were already bound to their destination.

The same-site rule is deliberately stricter than the stdlib's. Go
compares hostnames only, ignoring scheme and port, so it will carry
Authorization from host:443 to host:9999 — a different service, and on
shared infrastructure potentially a different tenant. That gap is not
visible from the request-building code either, because the redirect is
followed inside a single http.Client.Do: by the time control returns the
header is already on the wire. So redirect policy moves into a
per-connection CheckRedirect that strips the header on any hop leaving
the endpoint's site, layered over whatever policy the caller set. Setting
CheckRedirect replaces the stdlib's ten-redirect default, so that cap is
reimposed explicitly rather than lost.

The subdomain allowance keeps the case the flag exists for working: a
hosting replica under the same domain, example.com to
replica.example.com, still authenticates.

Tests cover the rule in isolation (including the near-misses: suffix
without a dot boundary, attacker-controlled prefix domain, scheme
downgrade, port change, IP addresses having no subdomains) and end to end
against httptest servers, asserting the cross-site POST carries no
credentials while a same-site redirect still does. Verified by hand too:
the original two-server reproduction that leaked the token now logs an
empty Authorization on both requests to the redirect target.

docs/usage.md gains a "Credentials and redirects" section — the flags
were previously documented only in their flag help.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git push -q -u origin soph/security-bind-token-to-host 2>&1 | tail -2
gh pr create --base soph/security-bounds-and-redaction --head soph/security-bind-token-to-host \
  --title "Bind explicit credentials to the host they were configured for" \
  --body "$(cat <<'BODY'
Fixes the highest-severity item left from the security review. **Stacked on #107** so the `smarthttp.go` changes don't conflict — the base is that branch, so this diff shows only its own changes. I'll rebase onto `main` once #107 merges.

## The problem

With `--source-follow-info-refs-redirect` / `--target-follow-info-refs-redirect`, git-sync adopts the host `/info/refs` redirected to and addresses it directly for follow-up RPCs — re-attaching the configured token to requests aimed at that host, *after* Go's `http.Client` had deliberately stripped `Authorization` on the cross-host hop.

Reproduced with two local servers, where the endpoint 307s to an unrelated host:

```
[LEGIT] GET  Authorization="Basic Z2l0OlNVUEVSX1NFQ1JFVF9QQVRfMTIzNDU="
[EVIL]  GET  Authorization=""                    ← stdlib stripped it
[EVIL]  POST Authorization="Basic Z2l0OlNVUEVS…" ← git-sync re-sent it
```

Any redirect an attacker can cause is enough: an open redirect on the real host, a hostile mirror, or a MITM on a plain-`http` source. On the target side the token usually carries write access.

## The fix

An explicitly supplied credential — token flags, bearer flags, or userinfo in the URL — now goes only to the host named on the command line and its subdomains, on the same scheme and port. Anything else gets nothing, plus a warning naming the withheld host, and the credential helper is consulted for that host instead:

```
source: withholding the configured credentials from http://localhost:64772/repo.git:
/info/refs redirected outside 127.0.0.1. Consulting the git credential helper for that host instead.
```

Credentials resolved *from* the helper are untouched — they're looked up keyed on the host being challenged, so they were already bound to their destination. The subdomain allowance keeps the case the flag exists for working: `example.com` → `replica.example.com` still authenticates.

## Why redirect policy moved into git-sync

The same-site rule is stricter than the stdlib's on purpose. Go compares hostnames only, ignoring scheme and port, so it forwards `Authorization` from `host:443` to `host:9999` — a different service, potentially a different tenant. My first version of the end-to-end test caught exactly this: both `httptest` servers are on `127.0.0.1`, so the stdlib happily carried the token across the port boundary and the test failed.

That hop isn't visible from the request-building code, because the redirect is followed *inside* a single `http.Client.Do`. So policy now lives in a per-connection `CheckRedirect` that strips the header on any hop leaving the endpoint's site, layered over whatever policy the caller set (theirs still runs and can still veto). Setting `CheckRedirect` replaces the stdlib's ten-redirect default, so that cap is reimposed explicitly — otherwise this fix would have introduced a redirect-loop hang.

The client is shallow-copied per connection, sharing the caller's `Transport`, so nothing the caller passed in is mutated or reconfigured.

## Tests

- `sameSite` in isolation, including the near-misses: suffix without a dot boundary (`notgithub.com` vs `github.com`), attacker-controlled prefix domain (`github.com.evil.example`), scheme downgrade, port change, and IP addresses having no subdomains.
- End to end against `httptest`: the cross-site POST must carry no credentials, and a same-site redirect must still carry them.
- By hand: the original two-server reproduction now logs an empty `Authorization` on both requests to the redirect target.

`gofmt`, `go vet`, `golangci-lint` (0 issues), `go test ./...` 17/17, `-race` on `gitproto` and `syncer`.

## Behavior change to be aware of

If a deployment today relies on the redirect target receiving the configured token and that target is **not** same-site with the endpoint, it will start getting 401s. The fix is to store those credentials in the git credential helper against the redirect host — git-sync will find them there. `docs/usage.md` gains a "Credentials and redirects" section explaining this; the flags were previously documented only in their flag help text.

BODY

Third of the remaining security-review items. **Stacked on #108** (which is stacked on #107); base is that branch so the diff shows only this change. Merge order: #107 → #108 → this.

## Why it matters

Nothing validated the names a remote advertises, and git-sync acts on them in two places where a malformed name bites:

**Written to disk.** `convert-sha256` passes advertised names to `SetReference`, and go-git resolves a name through the repository filesystem. Verified against go-git: `refs/heads/../../../../tmp/PWNED` lands at `<repo>/tmp/PWNED`, and `refs/heads/sub/../../../PWNED2` at `<repo>/PWNED2`. go-billy clamps traversal at the repository root, so this is repository corruption rather than arbitrary file write — but `config`, `HEAD`, and `packed-refs` are all reachable, with content constrained to an object hash.

**Embedded in receive-pack commands.** go-git's `formatCommand` writes the name verbatim, and receive-pack reads a feature list from everything after the first NUL on a command line. So a source advertising a name containing NUL injects capabilities into the push git-sync sends to *your* target.

`govulncheck` also flagged this call site under **GO-2026-6214**; #106 took the upstream fix, but validating at the trust boundary is git-sync's own job and also covers the push side, which the upstream fix does not.

## Approach

Validation defers to `plumbing.ReferenceName.Validate` — go-git's implementation of git's `check_refname_format`. I checked its coverage empirically before relying on it; it rejects `..`, NUL, CR, LF, other control characters, DEL, space, `~^:?*[`, backslash, `@{`, a `.lock` suffix, a leading dot, empty components, and a leading dash on a branch or tag. Deferring rather than hand-rolling keeps git-sync's notion of a valid ref identical to git's, so nothing git accepts gets skipped — confirmed against `refs/pull/*`, `refs/notes/*`, and nested branch names.

It runs at the two **decode boundaries** (`AdvRefsToSlice`, `decodeV2LSRefs`) rather than at each call site, so every path that reads an advertisement is covered by construction — source and target both. A skipped target ref is also one the planner never sees, so it's never picked as a prune candidate: the safe direction.

## Skip vs fail

Advertised names are **skipped with a warning**, matching how per-ref push rejections behave under `BestEffort` — one malformed ref upstream shouldn't stop a mirror. The warning names what was dropped so the divergence isn't silent, prints names with `%q` (they're remote-controlled, and an embedded escape sequence would otherwise reach the terminal), and caps the individual list while the count still covers everything.

`--map` values get the same validation but are **rejected outright**. They're configuration, and a mapped target ref reaches the same places an advertised one does, so failing at startup beats silently not mirroring what was asked for. Note this also closes the short-name form, where `--map main:../../config` becomes `refs/heads/../../config` after the prefix is added.

## Tests

- Every dangerous shape is covered individually with the reason it matters: parent traversal, traversal mid-path, NUL feature-list smuggling, CR, LF, ANSI escape, leading dash, `.lock` suffix, `@{0}`. Each asserts the *valid* ref alongside it still survives.
- Legitimate names must not regress: nested branches, tags, `refs/notes/commits`, `refs/pull/42/head`, `refs/merge-requests/7/head`.
- The warning must not leak raw control characters, must truncate, and must count everything.
- Mapping validation, including the short-name path.

## Behavior change to be aware of

If a source currently advertises a ref name git would reject, that ref stops being mirrored and a warning names it. Previously it would have been attempted and — depending on the target — either rejected server-side or written somewhere unintended.

Enforce the materialized object limit while the pack streams

FetchToStore filled the in-memory store with no cap. The object limit
(--materialized-max-objects, default 500,000) was checked against the
object closure once the fetch had already finished, so it reported an
overrun rather than preventing one: by then the objects were resident and
the process may have died getting there. The constant's own comment says
"fail early rather than OOM", which the ordering did not deliver, and
README's "guarded by an explicit object-count limit" overstated it.

failing the write that would exceed the limit. RawObjectWriter is the
choke point: go-git's pack scanner routes every object through it, and
memory storage's implementation only reaches SetEncodedObject via its own
internal closer, which never passes back through the wrapper — so
counting in both places would risk double-counting rather than add
coverage. Reads pass straight through, leaving planning and the push path
seeing the store exactly as before.

already configured and documented, so this changes when the existing
limit bites, not what the limit is.

The release workflow now attests the archives and the checksum file with `actions/attest-build-provenance`, recording a signed statement tying each artifact to this repository and the workflow run that built it. Verification needs no key distribution or keyserver:

```bash
gh attestation verify git-sync_<version>_<os>_<arch>.tar.gz --repo entireio/git-sync
```

Details:

- Adds `id-token: write` and `attestations: write` to the release job, which the attestation needs for its OIDC identity, alongside the existing `contents: write`.
- The action is pinned by SHA (`v4.2.2`), matching the convention in every other workflow here.
- The step runs **after** goreleaser, so a failure in it leaves a published release without provenance rather than blocking the release itself. That seemed the right trade — I'd rather not have a new step able to fail a release.
- README gains a "Verifying a download" section next to the install instructions.

I chose attestation over cosign keyless signing because it needs no extra binary in the release environment and verification is a single `gh` command users already have. If you'd prefer a detached cosign signature on `checksums.txt` as well (more portable for people without `gh`), that's a small addition on top.

## Verification status — read this bit

**This one I could not verify end to end.** The release job only runs on a tag push, so nothing here has executed. What I did check:

- The workflow YAML parses, and the job's step list and permissions resolve as intended.
- The action SHA matches the current `v4.2.2` tag.
- `go test ./...` still passes (18/18), though no Go code changes in this PR.

The first tagged release after this merges is what actually confirms it. If the step fails there, the release itself still succeeds — it just won't carry provenance, and the fix would be a follow-up rather than a revert.

| PR | Finding | Severity | CI |
|---|---|---|---|
| [#107](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/107) | allocation bound, SSH quoting, redaction, read caps, permissions | Critical + High + 4 | ✅ |
| [#108](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/108) | explicit tokens bound to their host | High | ✅ |
| [#109](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/109) | ref-name validation | Medium | ✅ |
| [#110](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/110) | object limit enforced while streaming | Medium | ✅ |
| [#111](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/111) | output sanitization + TLS-flag derivation | Low ×2 | ✅ |
| [#112](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/112) | release provenance | Low | running |

Each is stacked on the previous one — `smarthttp.go` and the CHANGELOG's `[Unreleased]` section are touched repeatedly, so branching off `main` would have meant six conflicts. Merge in numeric order and each rebases itself away. #106 is already merged.

Three things from doing the work rather than the review:

**The redirect fix needed more than my report said.** My same-site gate alone wasn't sufficient — my own end-to-end test failed on the first attempt because Go's redirect rule compares *hostnames only*, so it forwarded the token from `127.0.0.1:A` to `127.0.0.1:B` inside a single `Client.Do`, before any code of mine could see it. Redirect policy had to move into a per-connection `CheckRedirect`. That in turn removes the stdlib's ten-redirect cap, so I had to reimpose it or the fix would have introduced a redirect-loop hang.

**Two findings turned out cheaper than estimated.** Ref validation needed no hand-rolled parser — go-git's `ReferenceName.Validate()` already implements `check_refname_format`, and I verified its coverage empirically (`..`, NUL, CR/LF, control chars, `.lock`, `@{`) rather than trusting it. And the object limit needed no new default: enforcing the *existing* 500k limit during the stream instead of after removed the product decision I'd flagged as blocking.

**One test failure was the point.** #110 broke `TestRun_IntegrationMaterializedLimitFailsClearly`, which asserted the old post-hoc message. That failing was the signal the guard had actually moved; I retargeted it at the new `ErrObjectLimit` sentinel, which is stronger than substring-matching anyway.

On verification: everything except #112 is proven by tests that fail against the pre-fix code — I checked that explicitly for the SSH quoting, the allocation bound, both hang fixes, and the token binding. **#112 I could not verify at all**: the release job only runs on a tag push, so nothing in it has executed. The YAML parses and the action SHA is right; the first tagged release is what confirms it. I said so in the PR rather than implying it was tested.

Two loose ends worth your call: Bugbot returned `neutral` (declined to review) on #108 and #110, the two with the most delicate logic — you may want to trigger it manually. And I found an upstream issue while tracing #110: go-git's `memory` storage passes the pack-declared object size straight to `SetSize`, the same remote-controlled value #107 bounds in git-sync's own storer. That's go-git's to fix; I noted it in #110 rather than patching around it, and it's worth reporting to them given you maintain there.

git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Address review: make the object budget per fetch, not cumulative

Bugbot found that boundedStorer charged every RawObjectWriter call
against one running total, while the store outlives a single fetch. The
materialized strategy refills tag objects into the same store the closure
was fetched into, and does so with nil haves — so the source resends
objects already present, and those writes consumed budget a second time.
A run whose distinct object count sat comfortably under
--materialized-max-objects could therefore fail with ErrObjectLimit.

The cap now applies per fetch: FetchToStore resets it before streaming,
via an ObjectBudget interface the store opts into, so no caller has to
remember. Counting distinct objects instead would need the object hash,
which RawObjectWriter does not have until the content has been written,
and would mean keeping a set of every hash seen — more machinery than the
guard warrants.

The honest consequence is that worst-case residency becomes the limit
times the number of fetches, which is two on the sync path. That is still
bounded, which the original ordering was not, and it avoids failing runs
that are within the limit. Both the code comment and the changelog say so
rather than implying a cumulative guarantee.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Only Bugbot reviewed — no Copilot on any PR. It found **six real issues**, all confirmed and fixed:

## #108 — three findings, one High

**URL userinfo still followed redirects.** The one I'd have been most annoyed to miss. `outgoingAuth` gated `c.Auth`, but `resolvedEndpoint` was `*c.EndpointURL` with only scheme and host replaced — so userinfo came along, and net/http derives Basic auth from `req.URL.User`. I reproduced it before fixing: `Basic dXNlcjpVUkxTRUNSRVQ=` reached the redirect target. Worse than the flag-token case because `outgoingAuth` never sees it, so there was no warning either — a silent leak. Both construction sites now route through one helper that drops userinfo off-site and warns.

**Default ports read as different sites.** A false negative rather than a leak — `https://host` vs `https://host:443` would withhold credentials from a genuinely same-origin replica. Normalized per scheme.

**The warning promised a helper that wasn't installed.** `newConn` only installed the credential helper when `authMethod == nil` — exactly the case where the token *isn't* withheld. So a `--source-token` user hitting a cross-site redirect got a bare 401 and my documented remedy didn't work. The helper is now installed alongside explicit tokens; same-site requests still short-circuit to the token.

## #110 — the object budget

`ensureTagObjects` fetches with `nil` haves into the store the closure already filled, so resent objects were charged twice and a run within the limit could fail. Budget is now per-fetch, reset by `FetchToStore` via an interface. The honest cost, now stated in both the code and the changelog: worst-case residency is limit × number of fetches (two on the sync path). Still bounded, which the original ordering wasn't.

## #111 — two findings, one High

**I sanitized the wrong string.** `Error()` returns the *wrapped* error, which is what the CLI prints:

```
Reason field  : "rejected[2K\rok refs/heads/main"     ← cleaned
Error() output: "…rejected\x1b[2K\rok refs/heads/main" ← what users saw
```

**And `\r` alone is enough to spoof.** My own test passed while allowing it, because it only checked for ESC. The policy is now split: `Writer` keeps `\r` for progress (prefix-bounded), `Text` drops it for one-shot messages that have no reason to move the cursor.

I caught it by reading the resulting history rather than trusting the four "ok" lines, and redid it sequentially against local refs. Real bug, right fix, and the `sameSite` test table covers the cases that matter. `go vet` and `go test ./...` pass on the branch. Two things I'd change before merge — both are false *negatives* (credentials withheld where they shouldn't be), so they break working setups rather than leak anything.

## 1. `http` → `https` on the same host is now treated as cross-site

`samesite.go:43` requires an exact scheme match, so `sameSite(http://host, https://host)` is `false` (verified directly). A plain-`http` endpoint that redirects to `https` on the same host — GitHub does this, and so does about every corporate reverse proxy — works today, because the stdlib carries `Authorization` when only the scheme changed. After this PR the token is stripped on that hop, and with `--follow-info-refs-redirect` on, `outgoingAuth` then withholds it from every follow-up RPC too. Result: a hard 401 on a config that works today, and the "store it in the credential helper" remedy doesn't apply, because the host didn't change.

The stated goal is "an https endpoint never leaks a token over plaintext http" — that's the *downgrade* direction only. Suggest allowing the upgrade:

```go
if !strings.EqualFold(orig.Scheme, dest.Scheme) &&
	!(strings.EqualFold(orig.Scheme, "http") && strings.EqualFold(dest.Scheme, "https")) {
	return false
}
```

The port normalization already handles 80 → 443. Either way this belongs in the "Behavior change to be aware of" section, which currently mentions only non-same-site *hosts*.

## 2. `guardRedirects` anchors on the user-typed endpoint forever

`smarthttp.go:363` closes over `EndpointURL` at construction, but the connection's effective endpoint moves — `setResolvedEndpoint` adopts the redirect host, and helper credentials are then looked up *for that host*. Any further redirect that never leaves the adopted host still fails `sameSite(EndpointURL, req.URL)` and loses its `Authorization`. Reproduced: endpoint 307s to host X, helper creds bound to X, X bounces `POST /repo.git/...` → `/final/repo.git/...`:

```
GET  /repo.git/info/refs              Authorization=""
POST /repo.git/git-upload-pack        Authorization="Basic Z2l0OkhFTFBFUkNSRUQ="
POST /final/repo.git/git-upload-pack  Authorization=""      ← stripped on a same-host hop
```

That's exactly the path the PR's own documented remedy sends people down, so it undercuts the fix. The credential is bound to the host the *request* was aimed at, which the callback already has: use `via[0].URL` instead of the captured `endpoint`. That's per-request accurate for the token case (identical when `requestURL() == EndpointURL`) and for the helper-retry case (`via[0].URL` is the challenge URL), and it lets the closure drop the captured endpoint entirely.

content.text:
The comments on #108 weren't just Bugbot's three — **nodo left a human review** with two findings I'd missed. Both were real, and both verified before I changed anything.

## 1. `http` → `https` on the same host was treated as cross-site

`sameSite` required an exact scheme match, so `http://host` → `https://host` returned `false` (and `:80` → `:443` too). GitHub and most reverse proxies redirect that way, and it works today because the stdlib carries `Authorization` when only the scheme changes. My fix would have turned a working config into a hard 401 — with the documented "store it in the credential helper" remedy inapplicable, since the host never changed.

nodo was right that my own stated rationale only justified blocking the *downgrade*. The upgrade is now allowed, via a named `schemeCompatible` helper so the asymmetry is explicit. What convinced me it's safe rather than merely convenient: for an `http` endpoint the credential was already going to that host in cleartext, so an upgrade strictly improves things — there's no configuration where withholding on an upgrade protects anything. Five new test cases, including that the allowance can't smuggle in a host or port change.

## 2. `guardRedirects` anchored on the user-typed endpoint forever

The more consequential one: it **broke the remedy the PR itself documents**. The closure captured `EndpointURL` at construction, but the effective endpoint moves — `setResolvedEndpoint` adopts a redirect host, helper credentials get looked up *for that host*, and then any further hop within that host still failed `sameSite(EndpointURL, …)` and lost its header. I turned nodo's trace into a test and confirmed it fails against the old anchor:

```
--- FAIL: TestGuardRedirectsAnchorsOnTheIssuedRequest
    credentials were stripped on a hop that never left the adopted host
```

`via[0].URL` is the correct anchor for exactly the reason given — it's what the request was actually aimed at, rather than connection-level state that has since moved. The closure dropped its captured endpoint and `guardRedirects` lost a parameter. I added one thing beyond the suggestion: a nil anchor fails closed.

## Also

While doing this, **#107 merged**, so I rebased the whole stack onto the new main; GitHub had already retargeted #108 to `main`. I've replaced #108's behavior-change section with an explicit kept/withheld table, since nodo noted it only mentioned hosts.

One process failure worth naming: my first two attempts at re-stacking were both wrong. The first used stale `origin/` refs and silently dropped fix commits; the second used a `merge-base` heuristic that duplicated a commit; a third hit zsh not word-splitting unquoted variables, so SHA lists became single strings. I caught each by reading the resulting history rather than trusting the "ok" lines. The stack is now rebuilt deterministically — each branch is its base plus exactly its own commits — with all nine commits present and verified: `gofmt`, `go vet`, `golangci-lint` clean, 18/18 packages, and all eight review-fix tests passing.

CI is running on the pushed stack; I'll report when it lands. Merge order is now #108 → #109 → #110 → #111 → #112.
